parts.context: A scheme manager explains how a city bike-sharing scheme works and how it has performed.

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. My name is David Kim, and I manage the city bike scheme. I've been asked to give you a short presentation on how it works, what it has achieved so far, and what we are planning for the future.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: I will also leave time at the end for questions, so please write down anything you want to ask.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: The scheme was launched three years ago with only five hundred bikes and thirty docking stations. Today, we have just over two thousand bikes and more than two hundred stations, covering almost all of the central districts.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: To use the scheme, you first download the app and register. You then scan the code on the bike to unlock it. The first thirty minutes of every journey are free, which is ideal for short trips across the city.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: If you plan to use the bikes regularly, it makes sense to buy an annual pass. It costs forty pounds and removes the time limit, so you can cycle for as long as you like without paying anything extra.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: We've been surprised by who uses the bikes. We expected students and tourists, but our data show that the largest group is commuters, who use the bikes to get from the train station to their offices.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: One reason for this is speed. In the morning rush hour, a bike is usually faster than a bus or a car over distances of less than five kilometres, and of course you don't have to look for a parking space.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: It's also had a noticeable effect on the environment. We estimate that the scheme replaces about eight thousand car journeys every week, which reduces both traffic and air pollution in the city centre.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: Safety is something we take very seriously. All our bikes have lights that turn on automatically, and we offer free helmets at selected stations. Even so, accidents do happen, and most of them occur at junctions.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: For that reason, the council plans to build more separate cycle lanes. Over the next two years, an additional twenty kilometres of lane will be added, with priority given to the busiest roads.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: We have also had some problems. In the first year, almost ten percent of the bikes were stolen or badly damaged. We solved this by adding a stronger lock and a tracking device, and the figure has now dropped below two percent.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: Another challenge is balance. In the mornings, many bikes end up in the business district, while the residential areas run out. Our staff have to move bikes around in vans, which is costly and not very green.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: To tackle this, we are testing a reward system. If you return a bike to a station that is nearly empty, you get a credit of fifty pence. The first results are encouraging.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM

transcript.text: Looking ahead, our priority is to introduce electric bikes, which are particularly useful in the hilly north of the city. The first two hundred will arrive in the spring. Thank you for listening, and I'll take your questions now.
transcript.speaker: MR KIM
